entries.clue: Tight arse hiding in view (6)

indicatorNotes.hiding in: Something hiding in a place has gone inside it, so the letters just found are buried within the ones named next.

blocks.note: to view something is to see it
a cur is a mongrel, and the insult transfers to a man the same way arse does

annotation.surface: A mean-spirited man keeping himself just out of sight.
annotation.walkthrough: Tight arse reads as one compound insult and the split comes after the first word, which is the whole difficulty of the clue's opening. Cur is Private Eye's workhorse for any word meaning a contemptible man.
annotation.definitionFit: Secure means fastened so that nothing will shift it, which is what tight says of a knot or a lid rather than of a budget.

entries.clue: Prick meets northern reject (5)

blocks.note: to spur a horse is to prick it with the rowel on the rider's heel
n is northern on any map or address

annotation.surface: An idiot taking up with a discard from up north.
annotation.walkthrough: Prick is a verb here, the thing done to a horse, not the noun the Eye usually means by it. The northern half is a single letter, which is why the first piece has to carry four.
annotation.definitionFit: To spurn an offer is to turn it away with contempt, so reject in its verb sense of refusing outright.

entries.clue: Tip of septic member getting blue – withdraw! (5,4)

indicatorNotes.Tip of: The tip of a thing is its far pointed end, so what is wanted is the letter the word finishes on.

blocks.note: the letter this word ends on
an arm or a leg is a member of the body
feeling blue is feeling low in spirits

annotation.surface: An infected limb turning a worrying colour.
annotation.walkthrough: Member is the Eye's favourite word and means nothing but a limb here, with septic keeping the picture medical. Tip asks for the letter at the far end of the word rather than the one at its top, which is where a down entry tempts you to look.
annotation.definitionFit: To climb down is to abandon a position you have taken in public, which is what withdraw means of a threat or a claim.

entries.clue: Party's left unceasingly arse over tip (5)

indicatorNotes.arse over tip: Arse over tip is head over heels, and an assembly that has gone head over heels is read from its bottom end up.

blocks.note: l is the short form of left
what goes on unceasingly goes on for ever

annotation.surface: A political party whose left wing carries on for ever and then falls over itself.
annotation.walkthrough: Party is the definition in its revelry sense, not the political one the rest of the sentence sets up, so left is a letter rather than a wing. Arse over tip is the Eye's version of head over heels.
annotation.definitionFit: A revel is a noisy celebration, so party in the sense of the event you throw rather than the outfit you vote for.

entries.clue: Understood there are no bounds to simplicity (8)

indicatorNotes.there are no bounds to: Bounds are the outer limits of a thing, so a word with none of them gives up the letters at its two ends.

blocks.note: the ten letters the wordplay works on, printed whole
the letters standing at its two limits, and the ones the clue says are not there

annotation.surface: A weary observation that there is no limit to how simple things can get.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue looks like fodder because the wordplay is one long word with its outer letters taken off. Bounds are limits in the sentence and two particular letters in the parse.
annotation.definitionFit: An implicit agreement is one taken as understood without ever being spelled out, the two words naming the same unspoken assumption.

entries.clue: Cops turn up during dinner getting physical? (7)

indicatorNotes.turn up: Turning up lifts letters back the way they came, and in a down entry that means reading them from the foot of the assembly upward.
indicatorNotes.during: What happens during a meal happens inside it, so those letters are set within the ones named.

blocks.note: dinner is the main meal of the day
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the plain-clothes detective branch of a British police force

annotation.surface: Detectives arriving in the middle of dinner and turning rough.
annotation.walkthrough: Getting physical promises violence and delivers a check-up. CID is the police force crosswords reach for when they want three letters, and here it arrives upside down because the entry runs down the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: A medical is the examination an employer or an insurer puts you through, which is exactly what Americans call a physical.

entries.clue: All your remaining cash to endure ex-Tory minister? (4,5)

blocks.note: to endure is to last
Penny Mordaunt was a Conservative cabinet minister until she lost her seat in 2024

annotation.surface: What you would hand over to put up with a Conservative who has lost office.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that any Penny would serve, and Penny Mordaunt is the one the surface has in mind. Endure supplies a verb where the phrase wants an adjective, which is normal once the pieces are only letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Your last penny is the final coin you have left, so it is all your remaining cash once everything else has gone.

entries.clue: Needing to get end away, a prick set out for island (5)

indicatorNotes.Needing to get end away: Getting something away is getting rid of it, and the end of a word is the letter it finishes on.
indicatorNotes.set out: Letters set out are laid down afresh, in whatever arrangement the setter has chosen for them.

blocks.note: six letters to work from, one more than the grid has room for
the last letter of the six, and the one sent away

annotation.surface: A randy fool setting off for an island in hope of sex.
annotation.walkthrough: Getting your end away is British slang for having sex, so the surface stays smutty while the wordplay hears end as a letter. Prick is the Eye's word for a fool and its anatomical joke at the same time.
annotation.definitionFit: Capri is the island in the Bay of Naples, so the bare word names it by its kind with nothing narrowing it further.

entries.clue: Ex-PM, combination of Cruz and Bush? (3,5)

blocks.note: Ted Cruz, the Republican senator for Texas, goes by his first name in headlines
a heath is open scrubby ground, bush of the uncultivated kind

annotation.surface: Two American Republicans blended into a single man.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves come off the same Washington shelf, and only the first is still a name once the wordplay starts: bush is the landscape, not the family. The question mark covers the fact that neither American is doing more than lending a sound.
annotation.definitionFit: Edward Heath, Conservative prime minister from 1970 to 1974, was known to everyone as Ted, so the name answers to ex-PM.

entries.clue: Smear fudge round testicles initially to produce flow (6)

indicatorNotes.fudge round: To fudge something round is to knock it about until it will serve, and letters knocked about do not stay in the order they came in.
indicatorNotes.initially: Initially asks for the letter a word starts with and nothing else of it.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
the first letter of the word, taken as instructed and nothing else of it

annotation.surface: Spreading fudge around a pair of testicles.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue means exactly what it appears to mean, which is Private Eye's usual cover for a plain anagram. Fudge is the instruction to mess the letters about rather than anything edible.
annotation.definitionFit: A stream is water on the move, so flow names it by what it does, taken as a noun rather than the verb the surface offers.

entries.clue: Being wed, concealing small bill is far from welcome (9)

indicatorNotes.concealing: What conceals a thing holds it out of sight inside itself, so those letters go within the ones already found.
indicatorNotes.small: Small asks for the word in the shortened form a clerk would write on a ledger line, not the whole of it.

blocks.note: a couple being wed are united
an invoice, cut down to the three letters it is filed under

annotation.surface: A newly married couple keeping a modest invoice out of sight.
annotation.walkthrough: Being wed is a state rather than a ceremony, which is what lets it hand over a word about joining. The bill is the kind a supplier sends, not the kind put before Parliament.
annotation.definitionFit: A guest who is uninvited is one nobody asked for, so far from welcome states the same thing from the host's side of the door.

entries.clue: Jerk I had – quite tasty (5)

blocks.note: a sap is a gullible fool, the crossword's standard one
I had contracts to I'd, and the apostrophe is dropped

annotation.surface: Rating some fool you once slept with as fairly appetising.
annotation.walkthrough: Tasty is British for attractive in the surface and means flavoursome in the definition, which is the swap the clue is built on. Jerk is the American insult and the crossword's sap is the same man.
annotation.definitionFit: Sapid food has a taste worth noticing, so quite tasty covers it — a word that survives now mainly in cookery writing and crosswords.

entries.clue: Big shot with the Spanish treasure, keeping quiet (Trump wants it badly) (5,5,5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is not a synonym at all but a clause identifying the answer by who is after it, which a setter may do when the reference is unmistakable.

blocks.note: a nob is a person of wealth and standing
el is the Spanish for the
keeping quiet is keeping the peace
a treasure is a thing prized above the rest

annotation.surface: A grandee sitting on Spanish loot and saying nothing whatever about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The last two pieces arrive in the clue the opposite way round from the answer, so the familiar phrase has to be assembled by ear rather than read off. Trump has lobbied in public for the award for years, which is what the bracketed aside points at.
annotation.definitionFit: Trump has campaigned openly and repeatedly for the award, so the aside names the one prize the letters spell.

entries.clue: Rubber party act by Frenchman? (6)

blocks.note: Con is how the Conservative party is tagged on a British election results sheet
to act is to do
M is the abbreviation of Monsieur

annotation.surface: A Tory getting up to something in the company of a Frenchman.
annotation.walkthrough: Three pieces in six letters, and the shortest of them is a courtesy title rather than a name. Rubber sits first and looks like an eraser or a bridge contest, which is what keeps the definition quiet.
annotation.definitionFit: A rubber is a condom in everyday slang, the material standing in for the thing made out of it.

entries.clue: Break by court, between two dates, which goes with the flow (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a relative clause describing the thing rather than a noun that could stand in its place, which is how a setter names an object by what it does.

indicatorNotes.between: What sits between two things has one of them on either side, so the pieces gathered here are fenced in by the pair named.

blocks.note: d is the short form of date, and this is the first of the two the clue asks for
a break between allies is a rift
to court someone is to woo them
the second of the pair, closing the sandwich

annotation.surface: A ruling handed down by a court in the gap between two calendar dates.
annotation.walkthrough: Court is the wooing verb, not the building the surface puts it in, and break is a falling-out rather than a holiday. The dates go from diary entries to a single letter apiece, which is the pair that arrives last.
annotation.definitionFit: Driftwood is wood the current has carried along and dumped, so going with the flow is literally the only thing it ever does.

entries.clue: Drug-taking Russian leader, ultimately bleeding-heart liberal! (7)

indicatorNotes.taking: A man taking something has it inside him, so those letters go within the name beside them.
indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately points at the end of the word, so only the letter it finishes on is wanted.

blocks.note: Lenin led the Bolsheviks and then the new Soviet state
E is ecstasy, the crossword's default drug
the letter this compound ends on

annotation.surface: A Russian revolutionary on drugs being written off as a soft touch.
annotation.walkthrough: Russian leader wants to be Putin and the letters want Lenin. Bleeding-heart is a sneer at a soft liberal in the sentence and is cut down to a single letter in the parse.
annotation.definitionFit: A lenient sentence is a mild one, and liberal carries that same sense of going easy rather than any party allegiance.

entries.clue: Ballsed up in the large community race (9)

indicatorNotes.Ballsed up: To ball something up is to make a mess of it, and a mess of letters is letters out of their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
a city is a community on the large side

annotation.surface: Something badly botched in a big town.
annotation.walkthrough: In the looks like the grammar holding a phrase together and is really five letters of the fodder, which is where the clue hides. Ballsed up keeps the Eye's register and does the shuffling without any softening.
annotation.definitionFit: Ethnicity is the descent and culture a person is counted as belonging to, which is what race names in everyday speech.

entries.clue: Experiences beginning of individuality in kinky speedos (8)

indicatorNotes.beginning of: The beginning of a word is the letter it opens with, and that is all this takes from it.
indicatorNotes.kinky: Something kinky has been bent out of true, and letters bent out of true come out in a different order.

blocks.note: the first letter of the word, taken as instructed and nothing else of it
anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: Somebody's personality showing through a pair of very tight swimming trunks.
annotation.walkthrough: Speedos are the brand of skimpy trunks British beaches name them all after, which is what kinky is leaning on. Experiences is the plural noun and not the verb, and settling that is what fixes the ending.
annotation.definitionFit: Episodes are the separate things that happen to a person, so experiences in the plural noun sense of events lived through.

entries.clue: Container to check shag's over (7)

indicatorNotes.over: Something turned over comes at you the other way about, so the letters just assembled run backwards into the grid.

blocks.note: to rein something in is to check it
the nap is the raised pile on a fabric, and a shag pile is a long one

annotation.surface: A box fetched in to make sure the sex has finished.
annotation.walkthrough: Shag is the carpet trade's word before it is anything else, and the surface is built to stop you reaching for that sense. Check is the horseman's rein rather than anything ticked or written.
annotation.definitionFit: A pannier is the basket slung over a bicycle or a pack animal, so container names it by the one job it does.

entries.clue: Kiss of life helps to get Irene waltzing (7)

indicatorNotes.helps to get: What helps to get a result supplies only a part of it, so only a part of the words that follow is wanted — a run of letters inside them.

blocks.note: seven letters running straight on across the gap between the two words

annotation.surface: Mouth-to-mouth bringing Irene round and back onto the dance floor.
annotation.walkthrough: Waltzing sits exactly where an anagram indicator would sit, and the letters it points at are already standing in the order they are wanted. Irene is a name the surface needs and the wordplay only reads through.
annotation.definitionFit: The kiss of life is the British name for mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, and anything given it is being revived — a renewal of what had stopped.

entries.clue: One quarter Scottish, they casually make cuts (6)

indicatorNotes.One quarter: A quarter of an eight-letter word is two of its letters; the clue does not say which two, and the pair it begins with is the pair that serves.
indicatorNotes.casually: Doing a thing casually is doing it with no regard for the proper order, so those letters land any way round.

blocks.note: the first two of its eight letters, the quarter the clue asks for
anagram fodder, four letters as printed

annotation.surface: People of part-Scottish descent trimming things without much care.
annotation.walkthrough: One quarter Scottish reads as ancestry and turns out to be arithmetic on the letters of the word itself. Only the back half of the wordplay is shuffled, which is why the entry never looks like an anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: To scythe a field is to cut it down in long sweeps, so the tool's name doing duty as a verb is to make cuts.

entries.clue: Mo's back (6)

blocks.note: British shorthand for a moment, as in hang on half a mo
the verb: to support a horse, a motion or a candidate

annotation.surface: Word that somebody called Mo has returned.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words in the clue and two of them are definitions, with the 's doing nothing but making a sentence of the pair. Mo looks like a name because it is capitalised at the start, which is free of charge to the setter.
annotation.definitionFit: A second is the briefest unit of time, which is what a mo means when someone asks you to wait one; and to second a motion is to back it.

entries.clue: Bush method of taking down a dictator, not hard – "Sonofabitch is dishonest!" (5,3,7)

indicatorNotes.not hard: Not takes away whatever follows it, and hard is a single letter on a pencil, so that letter comes out of the word in front.

blocks.clueFragment: method of taking down a dictator
blocks.note: shorthand is how a secretary takes down the words of somebody dictating
h is the grade stamped on a hard pencil, and it is the letter lifted out of the nine above
a cur is a mongrel, and the word does the same work as the insult in quotes
somebody dishonest lies

annotation.surface: An American president explaining how easily a dictator was toppled, with a parting insult.
annotation.walkthrough: Bush is the definition and the only word of the clue that has nothing to do with American foreign policy. Taking down is dictation rather than deposition, and the dictator is simply the man reading the letter out.
annotation.definitionFit: The short and curlies are pubic hair, which is the bush of the definition; having someone by them is British for having them helpless.

entries.clue: Balls and member hard – that's vigour! (5)

blocks.note: a ball is drawn as a circle, and the clue asks for a pair of them
MP is a Member of Parliament, which is what member means in most British clues
h is the grade stamped on a hard pencil

annotation.surface: An anatomical inventory offered as proof of somebody's energy.
annotation.walkthrough: Member is the Commons abbreviation and the anatomy the sentence wants at the same time, which is the Eye's standard double. The balls are two circles on the page and nothing the sentence is about.
annotation.definitionFit: Oomph is the get-up-and-go that makes a thing go with a bang, an informal word for vigour.

entries.clue: Come again on meeting bastard (5)

blocks.note: re is on in the sense of on the subject of, the word at the head of a memo
a cur is a mongrel dog, and the insult for a man to match

annotation.surface: Turning up once more for another meeting with some swine.
annotation.walkthrough: Re is the crossword's usual way of getting two letters out of on, and it is the memo heading rather than anything Latin. Cur does duty twice in this puzzle, once as an arse and once as a bastard.
annotation.definitionFit: To recur is to happen a second time, so come again in the sense of coming round again rather than of asking someone to repeat themselves.

entries.clue: Sun-originated, maybe also Republican (5)

indicatorNotes.maybe: Maybe offers the letters as one possible arrangement of themselves rather than the printed one, which is about as light as a shuffle signal gets.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters
R is the letter printed after a US politician's name to mark the party

annotation.surface: Wondering whether something that came out of the Sun is Republican as well.
annotation.walkthrough: Sun is capitalised so that it reads as the tabloid, and the definition takes it as the star. Republican is a single letter here, which is the piece most likely to be mistaken for more of the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Solar means of or coming from the sun, so sun-originated is that adjective spelled out the long way round.

entries.clue: Dope mum has ball (5)

blocks.note: keeping mum is keeping silent, which is what dumb meant before it meant stupid
a ball is drawn as a circle

annotation.surface: An idiot's mother holding on to a ball.
annotation.walkthrough: Mum is the silence of mum's the word rather than the mother the sentence offers, and that swap is the whole of the misdirection. Dumbo was Disney's flying elephant before the playground turned it into an insult.
annotation.definitionFit: A dumbo is a fool, which is what dope means of a person rather than of a drug.

entries.clue: Turn Conservative and rise – it'll make you so much cooler! (4,5)

annotation.definition: it'll make you so much cooler

blocks.note: to wind a handle is to turn it
C is the Conservative tag beside a candidate's name
a rise in the ground is a hill

annotation.surface: Switching to the Conservatives and climbing the greasy pole.
annotation.walkthrough: Cooler is the definition's joke — colder, not more stylish — and the exclamation mark is there to sell the wrong sense. Turn is the verb for winding a handle rather than for changing sides.
annotation.definitionFit: Wind chill is the extra cold you feel when moving air strips the heat off your skin, so it does literally make you cooler.

entries.clue: Bloke had to enter cryptic clues programme (8)

indicatorNotes.to enter: To enter a thing is to go inside it, so the letters just gathered are planted within the others.
indicatorNotes.cryptic: Something cryptic has been put into a form you cannot read straight off, which for letters means out of their printed order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
a bloke is a he
had contracts to the 'd of he'd

annotation.surface: A man obliged to go in for a cryptic crossword competition.
annotation.walkthrough: Programme is a broadcaster's word in the sentence and a timetable in the answer, so the definition hides by being last. Had gives up one letter only, the apostrophe-d that is left when the word is contracted.
annotation.definitionFit: A schedule is the timetable saying what happens when, which is what a programme of events sets out.

entries.clue: Litany from Trump: "war ends!" – yeah, right! (6)

indicatorNotes.ends: The end of a word is the letter it finishes on, and this one is called on for both of the words in front of it.

blocks.note: the letter the name finishes on
the letter this word finishes on, the second of the two ends called for
aye is yes, the yeah of a voice vote
r is the short form of right, as on a stage direction

annotation.surface: Trump announcing that the wars are over, and being met with open disbelief.
annotation.walkthrough: Ends does double duty, taking a letter off Trump as well as off war, and the first of those is easy to miss because the name looks like the speaker rather than fodder. Yeah, right is the sarcasm and three of the letters at once.
annotation.definitionFit: A litany is a prayer of set petitions said in response, so the definition names one particular kind of the thing the answer covers.
